rationale: A wins because it keeps the strongest story grounded: "Glossier spent a decade as DTC-only. Wholesale is now its fastest-growing channel." It names the proof gap before a reporter does. B has the same basic instinct, but "The DTC darling that quietly became a wholesale company" turns fastest-growing channel into company identity, then inflates it into "the collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis." That's how a usable angle gets dressed up in a thesis costume and loses the room.
gaps_in_A: "Twelve years from beauty blog to 1,400 retail doors" is the softest viable angle; without principal access and one non-PR inflection point, it becomes a company retrospective with a news peg stapled on.
"The beauty brand born on a blog is coming to Kohl's" depends on the Sephora-at-Kohl's split; if only a small slice of the 800 new doors are Kohl's, the contrast collapses.
"Glossier was built as the proof case for direct-to-consumer beauty" imports a market-memory premise not in the update; it needs external support before the contrarian frame is bulletproof.
gaps_in_B: "quietly became a wholesale company" is overclaimed. Fastest-growing channel does not mean wholesale is the dominant channel, especially when the company discloses no revenue.
"covering the collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" invents a market-wide collapse from one brand's expansion. That's not an angle; that's a TED Talk looking for facts.

"A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" makes the weakest fact the protagonist. Three unnamed products and a vague "line extension" are not enough for a standalone fragrance story.

"direct evidence against the belief that digitally-native brands win by owning the customer relationship" overstates what the supplied facts prove; it needs market data or comparable brands, not just Glossier's line.
